text:
The summer I was fourteen, my father decided that I should learn to tie a proper Windsor knot, make a Negroni, and recognize, from across a crowded room, the exact moment when a man had stopped listening to the person he was talking to. These were the skills, he said, that would carry me through life. My mother, in Scottsdale, was teaching me to parallel park in her husband's Buick.

My parents had divorced when I was six, and I spent the school year in Arizona and July and August in New York, in my father's one-bedroom on West Twenty-third Street, where I slept on a daybed. My father, Daniel Roth, was forty-nine. He sold advertising space for a magazine about restaurants, and he entered rooms as if they had been waiting for him and were a little annoyed at how long he'd taken. At the airport he always held up a handwritten sign that said MISS JOSEPHINE ROTH, and he always bowed.

I was Josie to everyone else. To his friends I was the Duchess, the Contessa, Little Miss Sunshine, and, once, after I told a man named Franklin that his shirt was doing a lot of work, Anna Wintour. I loved this. At school I was a person who stood near other people and laughed a half second after they did. In my father's apartment I was an event. His friends arrived with gifts, asked what I thought of things, and then waited for the answer.

I understood, the way you understand things at that age, as weather rather than fact, that I was being fitted into something. There was a shape to my father's life, and it had a place for me, and I was working hard to be the right size. I learned which of the men were couples and which were "friends," and which couples were "open." I learned not to ask about the men whose photographs had gone from the refrigerator to a box on the closet shelf. At fourteen I had the manner of a small, tired diplomat.

What I did not let myself learn was why my father had gotten so thin.

---

The cruise was his idea, announced in May over the phone. Seven days out of Fort Lauderdale, the whole ship chartered. Eight hundred men, he said. Maybe nine hundred. "And you, my darling, would be the only one with a curfew."

My mother did not like it. I could hear her not liking it from the next room, in the low, rapid voice of a woman reading from a document. But she had a way of yielding to my father that she'd never had when they were married, a softness I think was grief she hadn't named yet, because by then she knew, too. She signed the form. She sent me with sunscreen and a laminated card with her phone numbers, which I put in my suitcase and never looked at.

We flew to Florida on a Saturday. My father wore linen and a straw hat and looked, from one angle, like a man in a cologne advertisement and, from another, like the drawing of one. In the taxi he fell asleep against the window with his mouth slightly open, and I watched the side of his face and did a kind of arithmetic with the bones in it.

The ship was enormous and white and stupidly cheerful, like a wedding cake that had been taught to float. A man in a sequined jockstrap and a sailor's cap took my picture without asking and then asked, with real anxiety, whether that was okay. He said I had marvelous cheekbones. My father, behind me, said, "She gets them from her mother," and I felt something move across my chest, quick and warm, like a hand.

---

By the second day I had a role: I was the one who knew where my father was. People stopped me in corridors. *Have you seen Danny?* I'd say he was napping, or that he'd be at the second seating, and the men would touch my shoulder and say, "You're a doll." I carried his pills in my beach bag next to my paperback, and every morning at nine I reminded him in a voice borrowed from a nurse on television.

"Yes, Mother," he said.

"I'm not your mother."

"No," he said. "She'd have been more annoying about it."

He played at being fine. He took a deck chair by the pool and let a dozen men make a court around him. I sat at the edge of the circle and saw that several of them were watching him the way I was: lightly, sideways, as if he were a pot that might boil over. At some point I understood that they all knew. This was what the trip was. Nobody said it, because saying it would have ruined it, and the point was to have a week in which it was not said.

I was furious for about an hour. Then, suddenly, I was not. A man named Marcus, who had a shaved head and a swallow tattooed on his neck and managed a hospice in Chicago, sat down next to me and handed me a Shirley Temple with three cherries. He just let me be fourteen next to him, and after a while he said, "Your dad talks about you constantly. It's boring. We all know your grades."

"I got a B-plus in geometry."

"We know," he said. "We *know*."

---

I met the boy on the fourth night.

His name was Eli. He was sixteen, tall in the stooped, apologetic way of tall boys, with a cowlick and a green T-shirt that said CAMP WINNIPESAUKEE. He was on the ship with his uncle, one of the hundred men I'd been introduced to and could not tell apart.

I was on the aft deck after dinner, alone, because my father had gone to lie down and the wake was a long white road disappearing into the dark. Eli was at the rail a few feet away. After ten minutes, he said, to the ocean, "Do you think they'd notice if we just stayed up here forever?"

"They'd notice," I said. "They'd throw us a party."

He laughed, a surprised laugh that got out before he could check it, and something about that made me want to say more. I told him I was good at being a girl among men who wanted me to be delightful, but that sometimes I wasn't sure if I was being myself or doing an impression of someone they'd like.

He listened with his whole face. At school, people listened the way you wait for a bus.

"My uncle's like that," he said. "At home he's quiet. He eats cereal for dinner. And here he's, like, *Oh my God, Eli, you have to meet Gary.* I think it's the same guy. He's just allowed to be loud here." He picked at the paint on the rail. "Is your dad sick?"

I had a great many answers prepared. *He's just tired. He's had a long year.* I opened my mouth to say one and what came out was, "Yes."

"Yeah," Eli said. "I figured. My uncle's friend was like that. Before."

He didn't say before what, and didn't have to. The ship hummed under our feet. After a while, without looking at me, Eli put his hand on the rail next to mine, not on top of it, just next to it, so that the sides of our little fingers touched. I would like to say I felt a great swoop of romance, but it was more like relief, the relief of setting down something heavy and discovering someone had been standing there, ready to take the other end.

"I'm not going to say anything dumb," he said. "Like it'll be okay."

"Thank you."

We stayed until the stars came out thick over the water. He told me he wanted to be a marine biologist, and that he was afraid of fish. I told him I wanted to be a person who said things in rooms and was listened to, and didn't know what that was called. "A lawyer," he said. "Or a woman." I laughed. He did not try to kiss me, and I was grateful, and a little sorry, and then grateful again for being sorry.

---

On the last night there was a White Party, and my father wore a white linen suit that now hung from his shoulders like a sheet on a line. I wore a white eyelet dress my mother had bought for my cousin's confirmation. The ballroom had become a cathedral for people who did not believe in cathedrals: white balloons, white drapes, a mirrored ball the size of a small car.

I expected my father to leave early. He didn't. He sat near the dance floor with Marcus, drinking club soda with lime, and received visitors like a bishop. Men knelt beside his chair to speak into his ear. I watched from the edge of the room with Eli beside me, the two of us holding paper cups of ginger ale.

Around midnight the DJ, a small woman in a white tuxedo, brought the room down. The beat stretched into something slower, a song I knew from my father's records, a woman's voice, a little ragged, singing about having had the time of her life. People drifted onto the floor, swaying.

My father stood up. It took a moment; Marcus half rose to help, and my father waved him off with two fingers. He crossed the floor slowly, and men moved out of his way the way water does. He stopped in front of me and bowed, as he had at the airport every summer of my life.

"Miss Josephine Roth," he said. "May I?"

I looked at Eli, who nodded once with great seriousness. I put my cup down on a stranger's table and took my father's hand.

He was not a good dancer, which I hadn't known. Now he simply held me and rocked from side to side. His hand was dry and light, like a leaf pressed in a book. Through the linen I could feel the narrow ladder of his ribs. I put my head against his chest and heard a small, quick, stubborn sound, like someone knocking and knocking at a door they were sure would open.

"You did all right this week," he said into my hair.

"I reminded you about your pills."

"You were relentless. I've never been so well managed." He was quiet for a few bars. "I wanted you to see that there's a place where people are like this. Where they just *show up* for each other. I wanted you to know it exists, so that when you're—" He stopped. I felt him decide not to finish. "So that you'd know where to look."

"I know," I said, which was not true yet, but would be.

Around us the men had made a loose circle, hundreds deep, and nobody was dancing except us.

"Don't let them tell you it was sad," my father said. "When you tell it. Promise me. Tell it right."

"How do I tell it right?"

"Tell them there was a disco ball. Tell them the food was terrible and I was the best-dressed man in the room."

"You were."

"I know," he said. "I really was."

The song ended. For a moment nobody moved, and then the room broke into applause, wild and ragged, a sound like rain on a tin roof, and my father, still holding my hand, turned and bowed to it, a real bow, and nearly lost his balance, and let me steady him. Then he laughed, and I laughed, and the DJ brought up something fast and silly, and nine hundred men in white began to shout.

---

He died in November, in a hospital on Ninth Avenue, on a morning when I was in Scottsdale taking a geometry test. There was a service in a rented room above a bookstore, and I wore the eyelet dress, too thin for the weather, and a man I did not know handed me his coat. Franklin spoke, and Marcus flew in from Chicago and said nothing, only held my face in both his hands for a long time. Near the back, in a suit that didn't fit, stood Eli with his uncle. He wrote to me for a year, long letters about fish, and I wrote back, and then, the way it goes, we stopped. I kept the letters in a box on a shelf, next to a laminated card with my mother's phone numbers that I never once had to use.

When people ask about my father, I tell them what he asked me to. The disco ball, the terrible food, the white linen suit. I tell them there was a week when I was fourteen and a ship carried me across a very warm sea, and nine hundred men knew my name. I tell them I learned to tie a Windsor knot and never learned to make a decent Negroni. And I tell them, because it's the part he'd have liked best, that at the end of the last night, in front of everyone, a man who was dying took his daughter's hand and bowed, and the whole room let him lead.
